The Round-tailed muskrat (Neofiber alleni) exhibits a suite of life-history traits characteristic of a semiaquatic rodent adapted to stable marsh environments. Neonates are born at a remarkably small size, with a birth mass of approximately 12 grams [Wwb = approximately 12 grams], reflecting the altricial state of the newborns. This low mass at parturition is typical among microtine rodents and places a significant energetic demand on the mother during the early lactation period. The gestation period that produces these altricial young lasts for 27.5 days [tg = 27.5 days] when measured at the species' core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This duration is relatively brief and falls squarely within the range of 26 to 29 days reported for this species, allowing for the potential production of multiple litters within a single favorable breeding season in the subtropical wetlands of Florida and southern Georgia.

Following parturition, the dependent young remain in the nest for a defined lactation interval before they transition to solid food. The onset of nutritional independence occurs at 15 days after birth [tx = 15 days after birth], a value determined under the standard thermal conditions of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This rapid weaning age is considerably shorter than that observed in many similarly sized arvicoline rodents, likely reflecting an adaptation to the high productivity of their marsh habitat, where emergent vegetation provides an immediately accessible source of nutrition for the emerging juveniles. At the point of weaning, the offspring have achieved a wet body mass of approximately 155 grams [Wwx = approximately 155 grams], although field data indicate this figure can range from 130 to 180 grams depending on litter size and maternal condition.

The growth trajectory continues rapidly after weaning, as the juveniles transition from a milk-based diet to foraging on stems and roots of aquatic plants. As the animals approach the end of their somatic growth phase, a pronounced sexual dimorphism in body size becomes apparent. The ultimate wet weight for adult females of this species has been recorded at 262 grams [Wwi = 262 grams], while their male counterparts achieve a greater final mass of 279 grams [Wwi = 279 grams]. This difference of approximately 17 grams is consistently observed across populations and is thought to be linked to intrasexual competition among males for access to breeding territories within the dense, elongate nests they construct from cattails and sedges. The larger body size of the male likely confers an advantage in agonistic encounters that occur during the breeding season. Adult body mass in both sexes is maintained throughout the year through continuous foraging activity.

At a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], individuals attain puberty at 45 days after birth [tp = 45 days after birth] and the maximum lifespan reaches 1898 days [am = 1898 days] under natural conditions. This remarkably early age at sexual maturity is one of the fastest recorded among North American rodents and allows for breeding to occur within the same season in which an individual is born, contributing to the species' high potential for population growth. Conversely, the maximum lifespan for this species is considerably longer than its short maturation time would suggest, spanning multiple breeding seasons.

The high reproductive potential of Neofiber alleni is further underscored by its reproductive output per event and the frequency with which those events occur. Females typically produce 2.2 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2.2 pups per litter], and they are capable of producing approximately 4.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 4.5 litters per year] under optimal marsh conditions. This annual reproductive schedule is sustained by a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], which facilitates the rapid metabolic processing required for the simultaneous demands of gestation and lactation. This output, when combined with the short generation time afforded by early puberty and rapid weaning, means that populations can recover quickly following periodic habitat disturbances such as flooding or drought. The species' ecology is intimately tied to the availability of stable, shallow-water habitats that support the lush herbaceous growth necessary for both food and the construction of their distinctive feeding platforms and lodges.
